title: What Toy Story 5 Gets Right (and Wrong) About Kids and Screens
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Katherine Martinko reviews Toy Story 5 as a cultural lens on children and screens, identifying five takeaways. First, Bonnie's parents are shockingly negligent—they hand her a tablet and barely notice as her personality shifts, failing to investigate even when she comes home visibly distressed. Second, tablets change the nature of play: they enable passive coexistence rather than active engagement, and battery-operated digital toys hold a child's attention for about two months while analog toys like Jessie endured for years. Third, online followers are not friends—Bonnie learns that group chats enable cruelty without consequence. Fourth, the imaginary play sequences (shown in pastel animation) are a reminder of what children lose when devices fill the hours. Fifth, the tablet gets an undeserved redemption arc, which Martinko rejects: parents should provide fierce, sustained refusal on their children's behalf, because children lack the capacity to resist on their own.
points: Bonnie's parents appear numb to the damage caused by the device, or willfully ignorant—even when she returns home visibly distressed and cries in the car over a group-chat incident.
Play and entertainment are not the same thing: tablets enable passive consumption and coexistence, while real play demands effort, focus, creativity, and imagination.
Analog toys endure years of imaginative reinterpretation; battery-operated digital toys command attention for about two months before the child loses interest.

Children have a brief window for deep imaginative play—they spend the rest of their adult lives fielding unanswered texts, but never have enough time to invent worlds—and parents should defend that window fiercely.
The tablet's redemption arc is the film's weakest point: parents owe children years of refusal because children cannot resist devices on their own.
quotes: Play and entertainment are not the same thing. Tablets distract through passive consumption, while real play demands effort, focus, creativity, and imagination.
Tablets appear to suck the energy out of a group of kids, who merely coexist in a space without actually engaging with each other.
Bonnie learns the hard way that just because someone “follows” you online or engages with you in a group chat does not mean that they are a real friend or even a good match for friendship.
Children have such a short window of time to lose themselves in such play; we should do everything in our power to protect that window and not let devices rob them of it.

We owe our kids a fierce defence. We owe them years of blatant refusal, precisely for all the reasons that are so wonderfully illustrated in the film—that kids do not possess the ability to resist on their own.
the device itself is not inherently bad, but the things it enables for children are.
